sources.title: Software Factories, Light and Dark (Addy Osmani)
sources.note: Not by Dex. Reports Dex's AIEWF talk: ~4 months of a fully automated factory with no human reading code, then painstaking manual debugging; review gate is the only non-scaling box; back pressure; agent holds 3-10 steps, loses thread past ~20; nightly cron fixing one anti-pattern per small PR; 'mostly deterministic code with LLM steps sprinkled in'. Osmani's own additions (types/seams/rubrics as outside-the-model safety net, 'what earns a loop the dark') are not Dex's and not carded. No direct critique of Dex found.

sources.title: Research, Plan, Implement, Review (Tyler Burleigh)
sources.note: Reports Dex's RPI as: fresh context between phases, markdown artifacts, 'Dumb Zone' (degradation past ~40% context), explicit compaction points, and implementation review optional. Burleigh critiques/extends with per-phase review, cross-model review, model routing, auto-compact off.

sources.title: Dex Horthy retracts Research-Plan-Implement (Dark Factory Dev)
sources.note: Paraphrase (unverified captions) of Dex's 2026-03 talk 'Everything We Got Wrong About RPI': ~10,000 people used the RPI prompts; he was wrong to advise not reading code (tried ~6 months, ripped out large parts); instruction ceiling ~150-200 (2025 paper), an 85-instruction mega-prompt plus CLAUDE.md plus tools overruns it and valuable steps are silently skipped; fix = split one prompt into smaller sequence; plan reading does not replace code reading; 8-page plan replaced by 2-page structure outline like a C header. The site's own note ('count what your harness actually loads before you add another skill file') is editorial, not a critique. Dex's retraction is his own idea: belongs to the talk reader, not carded here.

sources.title: AIEWF Daily Dispatch: The great loops debate (Latent Space, Richard MacManus)
sources.note: Reports Dex as skeptic in a loops debate: not anti-loops, Kubernetes control loops are deterministic; 'hype is outrunning the discipline'; step DOWN an abstraction level; with full automation 'you never touch the problem'; start small and build intuition. Opposing side (Huntley, Livingstone) and co-skeptic Pstrucha carded.

sources.title: Software Factories: Harnessing Loops At Scale (Hungry Minds newsletter)
sources.note: Pure summary of the Osmani piece, including Dex's four-months-dark-factory experience and the nightly one-lint-fix cron. No critique; nothing carded.

sources.title: On 'Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases' (Trey Causey)
sources.note: Endorsement only. Quotes Dex: frequent intentional compaction, utilization kept in 40%-60% range depending on complexity. No critique; nothing carded.

sources.title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases (comments on ace-fca)
sources.note: Full thread read (417 lines). Dex replies as dhorthy: Stanford slide on cases where AI made people slower; vim analogy; Go/typed feedback loops via integration tests; ~$650 raw tokens for 2 BAML PRs, team of three ~ $12k/month on Opus, then moved to Max plan; Claude Code injects a 'may not be relevant' system-reminder around CLAUDE.md; never use /compact, stash context to markdown or a git commit message and clear; 'read the entire file' instructions matter more than file size; 'the model can write the code but you still have to design it'; one failure (a plan wrong because types/SDKs were generated from OpenAPI, missed in research); hadoop refactor failed; no strong evidence for design-doc step. Critique-bearing comments carded.

cards.source_title: Research, Plan, Implement, Review (Tyler Burleigh)
cards.author: other
cards.quote: RPI treats implementation review as optional, while this playbook builds review into every phase transition
cards.claim: Burleigh criticises RPI for leaving implementation review optional and adds a new-session senior-engineer review plus fix loop after every research, plan and implementation stage.
cards.evidence_detail: His own workflow description; no numbers. Review steps: research review, plan review, implementation review each in a fresh session, then a final whole-branch review and optional refactor review.
cards.landing: Phase routine: per-phase Opus reviewer already exists; could add review of the research/plan artifact itself before implementation starts.
cards.inventory_ref: (C) Follow-ons and coverage by others (NOT Dex's work)

cards.source_title: Research, Plan, Implement, Review (Tyler Burleigh)
cards.author: other
cards.quote: A fresh session resets the context window but not the model's tendencies.
cards.claim: A fresh-context reviewer of the same model shares the implementer's blind spots, so independence needs a different model, different permissions (reviewer read-only) and automated gates passing before review.
cards.evidence_detail: Argued by analogy to ensembling in ML ('largely uncorrelated errors'); no measurement. Also proposes structured handoff (change summary plus diff, not the conversation) so the reviewer is not anchored.
cards.landing: Reviewer spec in ship plan: refute-by-default Opus reviewer is same family as implementer; consider a different-model or read-only-permission reviewer and diff-plus-summary handoff.
cards.inventory_ref: (C) Follow-ons and coverage by others (NOT Dex's work)

cards.source_title: Research, Plan, Implement, Review (Tyler Burleigh)
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Use your strongest model for research, planning, and review; use a faster, cheaper model for implementation.
cards.claim: Model capability should be routed by stage: strong model for synthesis and judgment stages, cheaper model for plan-guided implementation, escalating when the cheap model struggles.
cards.evidence_detail: Practitioner heuristic, no numbers or benchmark; contrasts with Dex's RPI which does not specify per-stage models.
cards.landing: Effort/model routing for verifiers and implementers in Workflow scripts; .claude/agents definitions with a model field.
cards.inventory_ref: (C) Follow-ons and coverage by others (NOT Dex's work)

cards.source_title: Research, Plan, Implement, Review (Tyler Burleigh)
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Turn off auto-compact (toggle in /config ). This lets you see when you're actually hitting context limits
cards.claim: Against strict context-percentage discipline, Burleigh keeps 200k models as default, disables auto-compact, and switches to 1M context only when stuck mid-task with no clean /clear path.
cards.evidence_detail: Cost figures quoted ($6/$22.50 Sonnet, $10/$37.50 Opus per Mtok beyond 200k, Feb 2026); no performance measurement of 1M versus fresh sessions.
cards.landing: Context budget note in phase routine: one phase per new session; 1M context as an escape hatch for long research sessions.
cards.inventory_ref: (C) Follow-ons and coverage by others (NOT Dex's work)

cards.source_title: Research, Plan, Implement, Review (Tyler Burleigh)
cards.author: other
cards.quote: the more detailed your plan, the more safely you can delegate to autonomous execution.
cards.claim: Safe autonomy scales with plan detail (high-level goal means human in loop each step; exact specs plus test cases means fully autonomous), cutting human touchpoints from about 12 to 2 (plan and PR), which tensions with Dex's later 2-page outline instead of 8-page plan.
cards.evidence_detail: A four-row table of plan detail versus autonomy level; the 12-to-2 touchpoint count is the author's estimate, not measured.
cards.landing: Ship plan phase spec granularity; decides how detailed a per-phase plan must be before an unattended run.
cards.inventory_ref: (C) Follow-ons and coverage by others (NOT Dex's work)

cards.source_title: Research, Plan, Implement, Review (Tyler Burleigh)
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Your time is expensive, tokens are cheap.
cards.claim: Burleigh argues extra sessions for research, review and revision cost more tokens but produce dramatically better results, so optimise for output quality not token efficiency.
cards.evidence_detail: No numbers; relevant counterpoint to cost-trimming of verifier effort.
cards.landing: Verifier effort policy: counterweight to lowering effort; needs the SlopCodeBench numbers to arbitrate.
cards.inventory_ref: (C) Follow-ons and coverage by others (NOT Dex's work)

cards.source_title: Research, Plan, Implement, Review (Tyler Burleigh)
cards.author: other
cards.quote: During review, ask the agent to identify where it may have over-engineered.
cards.claim: Models over-engineer by default (unrequested abstractions, impossible-case error handling, config where constants would do), so scope must be stated up front and checked in review.
cards.evidence_detail: Listed failure patterns from the author's practice; no counts.
cards.landing: Reviewer checklist item in the PR review prompt (over-engineering / scope creep check).
cards.inventory_ref: (C) Follow-ons and coverage by others (NOT Dex's work)

cards.source_title: AIEWF Daily Dispatch: The great loops debate (Latent Space)
cards.author: other
cards.quote: It's inevitable, it's here to stay
cards.claim: Pro-loop debaters (Huntley, Livingstone) counter Dex's caution: loops are already here, and verifiability, achievable for any code however produced, is what matters rather than stepping down an abstraction level.
cards.evidence_detail: Debate remarks relayed second-hand; no data. Huntley himself concedes software factories are 'frontier thinking' and not yet solved.
cards.landing: Nowhere obvious; framing for how far Workflow-script autonomy is allowed to run unattended.
cards.inventory_ref: (C) Follow-ons and coverage by others (NOT Dex's work)

cards.source_title: AIEWF Daily Dispatch: The great loops debate (Latent Space)
cards.author: other
cards.quote: orchestrate your problems away by buying more tokens
cards.claim: Co-skeptic Pstrucha argues agentic loops are economically unsustainable: more tokens do not substitute for orchestration discipline.
cards.evidence_detail: One paraphrased remark; the same piece cites an Amplify survey: 40% say AI cost regularly limits ambition and token usage is the second most monitored production metric.
cards.landing: Cost tracking per phase/workflow; supports effort routing.
cards.inventory_ref: (C) Follow-ons and coverage by others (NOT Dex's work)

cards.source_title: AIEWF Daily Dispatch: The great loops debate (Latent Space)
cards.author: other
cards.quote: bottlenecked on reviews
cards.claim: Even Anthropic's most delegated internal use (Krieger on Claude Tag) reports the human review and ability to conceptualise the work as the bottleneck, consistent with Dex's review-gate argument but a measured counter to 'just add agents'.
cards.evidence_detail: Single remark in a Krieger interview as reported; 59% of Amplify survey respondents fear AI code creates long-term liabilities.
cards.landing: Review-gate capacity planning for the owner view: one-page summary per PR.
cards.inventory_ref: (C) Follow-ons and coverage by others (NOT Dex's work)

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Agents __SHOULD NOT__ verify their own code.
cards.claim: CuriouslyC argues for a separate red-team reviewer agent and a panel of narrowly focused reviewers (security, performance, correctness, architecture) given code context plus the diff, rather than one all-purpose reviewer.
cards.evidence_detail: Says he has run this with Gemini 2.5 for about 6 months; catches line/module logic issues and anti-patterns but not big architectural ones. A commenter notes Codex /review runs in a subthread seeing only the git diff.
cards.landing: Reviewer design: split the single Opus reviewer into focused reviewers (custom agents) with diff-only context.

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Importantly, this code critic is wrong about 60% of the time.
cards.claim: iambateman reports an LLM plan critic produces false findings about 60% of the time, so a human must filter the critique before it is acted on.
cards.evidence_detail: Self-reported rate from his /feature workflow (8-10 markdown plan files, then a critic step); not a controlled measurement.
cards.landing: Supports refute-by-default and a refuter pass over reviewer findings; informs how much to trust unfiltered reviewer output.

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: I find it hard to read unverifiable documentation.
cards.claim: madcocomo critiques the research/plan stage: hours of planning with no running code to verify against is hard to trust, and a markdown file may not carry enough to the next stage; he prefers fresh sessions on small source-level problems.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal experience only.
cards.landing: P1 cold-resume trial: tests whether artifacts alone carry state across sessions.

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: most of the shenanigans of manual context window managing with putting things in markdown files is kind of unnecessary.
cards.claim: jgilias reports Cursor's automatic todos and summarising compaction made manual context management mostly unnecessary, challenging the frequent-intentional-compaction thesis (Dex replied elsewhere: never use /compact, stash context to markdown or a commit message and clear).
cards.evidence_detail: Single user, Sonnet 4 in Cursor; plans and guided research still needed. Dex's reply in-thread: you want control and visibility over what is compacted.
cards.landing: Phase routine rule 'one phase per new chat' versus tool-side auto compaction; decisions journal as the stash.

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: You can have a huge codebase, but if the complexity goes up with size then you are screwed.
cards.claim: philipp-gayret disputes the 'performance / size' framing (complexity, not size, matters) and doubts that one bad CLAUDE.md line is 100K bad lines; Dex replies that Claude Code wraps CLAUDE.md in a 'may not be relevant' system-reminder so a poor CLAUDE.md is probably survivable.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's reply quotes the injected system-reminder text ('this context may or may not be relevant... Most of the time, it is not relevant') and says if you do not know what is in your context window you cannot balance CLAUDE.md against commands.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim decision: the wrapper explains why long CLAUDE.md content is down-weighted; supports moving rarely-needed invariants out of always-loaded context.

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: it always diverges into researching and proposing fixes as well as searching for root causes
cards.claim: jarek83 reports Claude Code frequently ignores the research_codebase prompt's explicit prohibition (document only, do not propose fixes), succeeding only twice in many tries, i.e. prompted phase constraints are not reliably followed.
cards.evidence_detail: Single user's tries; no Dex answer in the file we read (thread ends there).
cards.landing: Evidence for hooks or checkable outputs rather than prompt-only phase rules; re-opens the skipped hooks decision.

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: I find models try to write scripts/manual workflows for testing
cards.claim: Exchange on why typed/compiled languages (Go) work better: compile steps plus LSP feedback improve agent output; Dex says Go is good for building the model's own feedback-loop harness via integration tests. Commenters (mholm, 0xblacklight) add stable idioms and richer types.
cards.evidence_detail: Opinions from commenters; Dex points to humanlayer/hld integration tests as an example.
cards.landing: Backpressure: mypy strict, import-linter and pytest are already gates; supports integration-test harness as agent feedback loop.

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: You can have two, and intermittently three, parallel process at once
cards.claim: OtherShrezzing (with scuff3d, noodletheworld) argues human spec/PR administration (about 8 minutes per ~20-minute agent block) caps parallel agent runs at 2-3, and context switching erodes the gains.
cards.evidence_detail: Back-of-envelope arithmetic (3 min spec plus 5 min PR per 20 min of agent work); the_duke replies 10 parallel is possible but 'not a sustainable pace'.
cards.landing: Workflow-tool fan-out sizing and owner-view budget: review capacity, not agent count, sets the limit.

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: a 20k LoC PR is an actively hostile move
cards.claim: Many commenters (ooopakaj, ActionHank, bak3y, sensanaty, wwweston) say giant AI PRs are unreviewable and should be closed in favour of small atomic PRs; yojo adds that LLM-written tests are often poor and 2k lines of test diff is itself too much.
cards.evidence_detail: Opinion plus yojo's example (five 200ms-wait tests added a second to the suite). Dex's reply: the model can write the code but you still design it; engage more, iterate, work in small steps.
cards.landing: PR size cap and test-quality check in the Opus reviewer prompt; fail-before/pass-after per register id already addresses tautological tests.

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: LLMs are categorically not compilers.
cards.claim: sothatsit, sarchertech and maltalex reject the 'specs are the new source, you stop reading code' claim: LLMs are non-deterministic, you must read code to confirm the right program was written, so it is delegation not abstraction (Dex later retracted the don't-read-the-code advice per DarkFactory).
cards.evidence_detail: Argument by principle; sarchertech reports a Claude Sonnet 4 trial of a CSV prompt (90-line script, float multiplication, loads whole file, crashes on currency symbols); qcnguy replies with a GPT-5 spec-review-implement run that handled the edge cases.
cards.landing: Owner-view and reviewer policy: code is still read at the gate; specs are not a substitute.

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Overall productivity boost at 15 - 20% IIRC.
cards.claim: malfist and others challenge the productivity premise, noting studies show AI can make some people less effective; keeda/CharlesW cite the Stanford analysis at about 15-20% average gain with slowdowns concentrated in high-complexity tasks on legacy or low-popularity languages, and Dex confirms the Stanford video has a slide on slower-than-no-AI cases.
cards.evidence_detail: Numbers are second-hand recollection of a Stanford video (average ~15-20%); not verified by the commenters, who say 'IIRC'.
cards.landing: Nowhere obvious; background for measuring actual benefit per phase rather than assuming it.

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: A 35k LOC change in a 350k codebase
cards.claim: daxfohl and others press on cost and measurement: Dex answers that 2 BAML PRs cost about $650 in raw tokens, his team of three averages about $12k per month on Opus, and they moved to a Max plan after running out of credits; gloosx notes '7 hours' versus 40 commits over 7 days (one 'ignore some tests'); afro88 notes only 2 of 3 tasks shipped.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's own figures given in reply ($650 for two PRs, ~$12k/month for three people); critics' counts: 40 commits over 7 days, one PR still draft over a month later, sample of 3 tasks in 2 codebases.
cards.landing: Cost per phase accounting in the closing message or owner view; claims of speed should state elapsed days, not hours of agent time.

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: really specific documentations were almost as if I was 'over-fitting' my solution
cards.claim: nzach argues detailed specs overfit and reduce quality (last 10-20% never right), preferring concise behaviour-focused prompts plus plan mode; boredtofears and apercu agree; Dex notes his create_plan prompt runs a 3+ phase clarifying-question exchange before writing the plan.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal experience of several commenters; the 'ask me clarifying questions' tip (danielbln, BeetleB) is offered as a cheap alternative.
cards.landing: Plan granularity in the phase routine: tension between detailed plan (R38-5) and over-specification; clarifying-question step before plan.

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: The problem is the research phase will fail because you can't glean tribal product knowledge
cards.claim: asdev argues research that only reads code cannot recover tribal product knowledge; Dex's own reply elsewhere admits a plan was wrong because research missed that types and SDKs were generated from an OpenAPI spec.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's anecdote: user story plus research plan existed, yet a missing fundamental detail surfaced only deep in implementation and the plan was wrong.
cards.landing: P1 cold-resume trial and knowledge store: facts that code reading cannot recover must be written down; generated-code provenance as a frozen fact.

cards.source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: your 200k LoC project could be solved in only about 10k LoC
cards.claim: LeafItAlone, jongjong and jwpapi argue agent output is needlessly complex and line-count claims are a bad metric; 'simplify the solution' is their most common instruction, and 35k lines of generated code is not a productivity measure.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenters' impressions (10k vs 200k guess is an estimate, not a measurement); Dex concedes 'wrote' rather than 'shipped' and that it is uncertain when to let duplication sprawl versus DRY.
cards.landing: Reviewer prompt: complexity/over-engineering check; avoid LOC as a progress metric in closing messages.

gaps: Dex's own talk 'Everything We Got Wrong About RPI' (2026-03) was only seen via the DarkFactory paraphrase (unverified captions); its claims (instruction ceiling ~150-200, 85-instruction prompt, split prompts, 2-page structure outline) are not carded here and belong to the reader of that talk.
Osmani, Hungry Minds and Trey Causey contain no direct critique of Dex; they were recorded in sources only, per the bundle notes.
The Latent Space dispatch is a second-hand account of the loops debate; Dex's exact words are not available from it.
HN thread was read in full (417 lines) but some comment text is truncated by the dump (e.g. the fragmede comment ends mid-sentence).
